results.title: Yennayer: North Africa's 3,000-year-old new year's celebration
results.content:
The Amazigh calendar starts at 950 BCE, when King Sheshonq ascended the throne of Egypt, meaning this year is 2974. For Amazigh communities in Morocco, this Yennayer will be particularly special. [...] On the evening of 12 January, dozens of bonfires burned on the rocky hillside above the village of Tisselday in Morocco's High Atlas Mountains. They were lit by families for Yennayer, the Amazigh (or Berber) new year celebrations. The fires symbolise a cleansing or purification of the past year, explained Ahmed Agouni, a trained geologist and owner of the long-running Irocha guesthouse in his home village of Tisselday, some 1,530m above sea level on the High Atlas eastern slopes. [...] Children should be warned, though. "We throw the candies gently on the heads of children so that it brings good luck and that the year ahead will be sweet," said Abdelli-Tancrede.

results.title: Amazigh New Year — CROSSROADS CULTURAL EXCHANGE
results.content:
This Amazigh New Year’s celebration is called “Yennayer,” the same name as the word for the first month in the Amazigh calendar. This word may be derived from the literal words in Amazigh for “first month” (Yan = One, and Ayyur = month). The beginning of this year corresponds to the first day in January in the Julian Calendar. So, 2974 Amazigh year corresponds to 2024 in the Gregorian calendar. This celebration of the new year is also called “ Id Suggas,” by Imazighen, which means “night of the [...] The Amazigh people (also known as Imazighen, or in English often called Berber\ people) were the original inhabitants of Morocco two thousand years ago. Originally nomads, now Imazighen often live semi-nomadic lives or have settled into towns and villages, but the language, traditions, and norms continue to be passed down across generations. One of these traditions is the Amazigh New Year, which begins the evening of January 13th every year. [...] \We intentionally try to avoid the term Berber, because this name was given to Imazighen people by foreign people, especially European colonizers, and was used as a derogatory term (meant to imply barbarian or uncivilized). The Amazigh people generally prefer to be known as Imazighen, or one of the other names for their specific regional people groups.

We’ll be able to answer this question more precisely once we know what Yennayer really is. But in the meantime, the fact that the ‘Julian’ New Year is now 14 January means nothing!

results.title: Why Is the Amazigh Calendar 950 Years Ahead?
results.content:
The idea of giving the Amazigh calendar its own year numbering emerged within Berber cultural circles in Paris during the second half of the twentieth century.

It is chiefly associated with Ammar Negadi, a Chaoui intellectual and cultural activist. In 1980, he published a calendar bearing the year 2930, calculated by adding 950 years to the Gregorian date.

The principle is simple: 1980 + 950 = 2930. In the same way, 2026 becomes 2976, 2027 becomes 2977, and so on. [...] This calendar helped mark the time for sowing and harvesting, periods of cold weather, and days regarded as favourable or dangerous for crops. Over time, it became enriched by local traditions, sayings, observations of the stars and practices specific to different regions of North Africa.

But the years were not numbered from some ancient Amazigh ‘year zero’. The practice of writing 2976, 2977 or 2978 today belongs to a much more recent history.

Read more: Yennayer, the Amazigh New Year [...] When a new Amazigh year begins at Yennayer, its year number is 950 years ahead of the Gregorian calendar: 2026 thus becomes 2976. This figure might suggest that Amazigh people have been counting the years in this way for almost three millennia. That is not the case. North Africa’s agricultural calendar is ancient, but the present-day numbering of Amazigh years is a twentieth-century creation.
